theory.intro: When a quadratic $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ has an unknown coefficient, called the **parameter**, the discriminant $\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$ becomes an expression in it. The condition for the number of solutions then gives an equation or inequality to solve. These discriminant conditions require $a\ne0$; check parameter values that make $a=0$ separately in the original equation.
facts: For $a\ne0$, exactly one real solution (equal roots) requires $\Delta=0$.

When the parameter appears linearly only in $a$ or only in $c$, with the other coefficients fixed and nonzero, $\Delta$ is linear in it. A single occurrence in $b$, or a nonlinear occurrence, need not give a linear discriminant.

When the parameter is the coefficient $b$ and the other coefficients are fixed, $\Delta$ contains its square. Depending on the other coefficients and any restrictions, $\Delta=0$ can give zero, one or two allowed real values of the parameter.
Reverse the inequality symbol when you divide an inequality by a negative number.
steps: Write the equation as $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$ and identify $a$, $b$ and $c$ in terms of the parameter. Check any parameter values that make $a=0$ separately in the original equation.
For $a\ne0$, form $\Delta=b^{2}-4ac$ as an expression in the parameter.
Solve the resulting equation or inequality for the parameter, keeping $a\ne0$, and include any separately checked values that meet the requested condition.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+16x+k=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=16,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=16^{2}-4(1)(k)\\&=256-4k\end{align*}$
For two distinct real solutions, $\Delta>0$.
$\begin{align*}256-4k&>0\\-4k&>-256\\k&<64\end{align*}$
Dividing by $-4$ reverses the inequality.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the value of $k$ for which $3x^{2}-18x+k=0$ has exactly one real solution.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=3,\ b=-18,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-18)^{2}-4(3)(k)\\&=324-12k\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}324-12k&=0\\12k&=324\\k&=27\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+k=18x$ has no real solutions.
workedExamples.solution_text:
Write the equation in standard form.
$x^{2}-18x+k=0$
$a=1,\ b=-18,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-18)^{2}-4(1)(k)\\&=324-4k\end{align*}$
For no real solutions, $\Delta<0$.
$\begin{align*}324-4k&<0\\-4k&<-324\\k&>81\end{align*}$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+kx+36=0$ has exactly one real solution.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=k,\ c=36$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=k^{2}-4(1)(36)\\&=k^{2}-144\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}k^{2}-144&=0\\k^{2}&=144\\k&=\pm12\end{align*}$
Both parameter values give a repeated real root.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $3x^{2}+kx+3=0$ has no real solutions.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=3,\ b=k,\ c=3$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=k^{2}-4(3)(3)\\&=k^{2}-36\end{align*}$
For no real solutions, $\Delta<0$.
$\begin{align*}k^{2}-36&<0\\k^{2}&<36\end{align*}$
The square of $k$ is less than $36$ precisely when $k$ lies between $-6$ and $6$.
$-6<k<6$

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $(k+3)x^{2}+2x-2=0$ has two distinct real solutions.
workedExamples.solution_text:
The equation is quadratic when $k\ne-3$.
$a=k+3,\ b=2,\ c=-2$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=2^{2}-4(k+3)(-2)\\&=4+8(k+3)\\&=8k+28\end{align*}$
For two distinct real solutions, $\Delta>0$.
$\begin{align*}8k+28&>0\\8k&>-28\\k&>-\frac{7}{2}\end{align*}$
When $k=-3$, the original equation becomes $2x-2=0$, with only one real solution, $x=1$.
Therefore $k>-\frac{7}{2}$ and $k\ne-3$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $kx^{2}-10x+k=0$ has exactly one real solution, given $k\ne0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=k,\ b=-10,\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-10)^{2}-4(k)(k)\\&=100-4k^{2}\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}100-4k^{2}&=0\\4k^{2}&=100\\k^{2}&=25\\k&=\pm5\end{align*}$
Both values satisfy $k\ne0$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}-(k+3)x+25=0$ has exactly one real solution.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=-(k+3),\ c=25$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-(k+3))^{2}-4(1)(25)\\&=(k+3)^{2}-100\end{align*}$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$\begin{align*}(k+3)^{2}-100&=0\\(k+3)^{2}&=100\\k+3&=\pm10\end{align*}$
Thus $k=7$ or $k=-13$.

workedExamples.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $kx^{2}-(2k-3)x+k=0$ has no real solutions, given $k\ne0$.
workedExamples.solution_text:
$a=k,\ b=-(2k-3),\ c=k$.
$\begin{align*}\Delta&=(-(2k-3))^{2}-4(k)(k)\\&=4k^{2}-12k+9-4k^{2}\\&=9-12k\end{align*}$
For no real solutions, $\Delta<0$.
$\begin{align*}9-12k&<0\\-12k&<-9\\k&>\frac{3}{4}\end{align*}$
Every value in this range satisfies $k\ne0$.

foundation.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+6x+k=0$ has two real solutions.
Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+10x+k=0$ has no real solutions.
Find the value of $k$ for which $2x^{2}+8x+k=0$ has exactly one real solution.
foundation.solution_text:
$a=2,\ b=8,\ c=k$
$\Delta=8^{2}-4(2)(k)$
$=64-8k$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$64-8k=0$
$-8k=-64$
$k=8$

foundation.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}+8x+k=0$ has two real solutions.
Find the value of $k$ for which $x^{2}-4x+k=0$ has exactly one real solution.
foundation.solution_text:
$a=1,\ b=-4,\ c=k$
$\Delta=(-4)^{2}-4(1)(k)$
$=16-4k$
For exactly one real solution, $\Delta=0$.
$16-4k=0$
$-4k=-16$
$k=4$

development.solution_text:

development.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $x^{2}-kx+25=0$ has exactly one real solution.
Find the values of $p$ for which $px^{2}+4x+2=0$ has no real solutions.
Find the values of $k$ for which $kx^{2}-4x+2=0$ has two real solutions.
development.solution_text:
$a=k,\ b=-4,\ c=2$
$\Delta=(-4)^{2}-4(k)(2)$
$=16-8k$
For two real solutions, $\Delta>0$ and $k\ne0$.
$16-8k>0$
$-8k>-16$
$k<2$
When $k=0$, the equation is $-4x+2=0$, which has only one real solution, $x=\frac{1}{2}$.
Therefore $k<2$ and $k\ne0$.

development.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $(k+2)x^{2}+x-3=0$ has two real solutions.
development.solution_text:
$a=k+2,\ b=1,\ c=-3$
$\Delta=1^{2}-4(k+2)(-3)$
$=1+12(k+2)$
$=12k+25$
For two real solutions, $\Delta>0$ and $k\ne-2$.
$12k+25>0$
$12k>-25$
$k>-\frac{25}{12}$
When $k=-2$, the equation is $x-3=0$, which has only one real solution, $x=3$.
Therefore $k>-\frac{25}{12}$ and $k\ne-2$.

development.question_text: Find the values of $k$ for which $2x^{2}+3x+k=0$ has two real solutions.
Find the values of $b$ for which $2x^{2}+x+b+1=0$ has two real solutions.
development.solution_text:
The coefficient of $x^{2}$ is $2$, the coefficient of $x$ is $1$, and the constant is $b+1$.
$\Delta=1^{2}-4(2)(b+1)$
$=1-8(b+1)$
$=-8b-7$
For two real solutions, $\Delta>0$.
$-8b-7>0$
$-8b>7$
$b<-\frac{7}{8}$
